```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4
)
has_ggplot2 <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
has_ggtern  <- has_ggplot2 && requireNamespace("ggtern", quietly = TRUE)
```

`rktool` analyses the rhythm of any sequence of events (calls, notes,
footsteps, keystrokes...) through **rhythmic ratios**. Starting from the
onset times of the events, it computes the intervals between them, turns
each pair of consecutive intervals into a ratio, classifies the ratios into
rhythmic categories and tests whether some categories occur more often than
expected by chance.

This vignette walks through the whole workflow on the example dataset
shipped with the package:

1. `calculate_tk()`: intervals from onsets;
2. `calculate_rk()`: rhythmic ratios from intervals;
3. `classify_rk()`: rhythmic bins of each ratio;
4. `count_rk()`: bin counts per group;
5. `compute_null_distributions()` / `simulate_null_runs()`: bin
   proportions expected under a null model;
6. `normalize_rk_counts()`: counts normalized against the null model (or
   the bin width);
7. `test_peaks()`: "on" vs "off" tests for each category;
8. `find_rk_peaks()`, `plot_rk_density()`, `plot_rk_ternary()`: exploration
   and plots.

```{r setup}
library(rktool)
```

## Key concepts

Given an interval $t_k$ and the following interval $t_{k+1}$ of the same
sequence, the **rhythmic ratio** is

$$r_k = \frac{t_k}{t_k + t_{k+1}}, \qquad 0 < r_k < 1.$$

Isochronous rhythms (two equal intervals) give $r_k = 0.5$; a short interval
followed by one twice as long gives $r_k = 1/3$, and so on.

- A **category** (or peak) is an integer ratio: `"1_1"` (1:1, centred on
  0.5), `"1_n"` (centred on $1/(n+1)$, e.g. `"1_2"` at 1/3) and `"n_1"`
  (centred on $1 - 1/(n+1)$, e.g. `"2_1"` at 2/3).
- Each category is split into two **bins**: `"on"`, the central part close
  to the integer ratio, and `"off"`, the two outer parts. Labels look like
  `"1_2_on"` / `"1_2_off"`.

A rhythm that really is organised around a category shows more `on` than
`off` values for it, once the different chance level of each bin has been
taken into account.

## The example data

```{r data-info, include = FALSE}
n_sex <- table(unique(data_rktool[c("ind_id", "sex")])$sex)
```

`data_rktool` contains the onset times (in seconds) of
`r format(nrow(data_rktool), big.mark = ",")` events annotated in
`r length(unique(data_rktool$file_id))` recordings, for
`r length(unique(data_rktool$ind_id))` individuals
(`r paste(n_sex, names(n_sex), collapse = ", ")`).

```{r data}
head(data_rktool)
str(data_rktool)
```

Each temporal sequence is a recording x individual combination, so in all
the steps below `by = c(file_id, ind_id)`. Column arguments accept bare
names (`file_id`) or strings (`"file_id"`), and those that accept several
columns take `c(...)`.

## 1. Intervals: `calculate_tk()`

`calculate_tk()` sorts the rows by onset within each sequence and computes
`tk = onset - previous onset`. The first interval of each sequence is `NA`,
because it has no previous onset.

```{r tk}
y <- calculate_tk(data_rktool, onset_col = onset, by = c(file_id, ind_id))
head(y[c("file_id", "ind_id", "onset", "tk")])
summary(y$tk)
```

If your data already contain the intervals, skip this step.

## 2. Rhythmic ratios: `calculate_rk()`

`calculate_rk()` computes `rk` between each interval and the next one of the
same sequence. The last interval of a sequence has no successor, so its
`rk` is `NA`.

```{r rk}
y <- calculate_rk(y, tk_col = tk, by = c(file_id, ind_id))
summary(y$rk)
```

Long pauses between bouts are usually not part of the rhythm. Use `tk_max`
to avoid computing ratios that involve an interval longer than a
threshold (here 5 s):

```{r rk-tkmax}
y2 <- calculate_rk(y, tk_col = tk, by = c(file_id, ind_id), tk_max = 5,
                   rk_name = "rk_5s")
c(all = sum(!is.na(y2$rk)), tk_max_5 = sum(!is.na(y2$rk_5s)))
```

The distributions of `tk` and `rk` can be inspected with
`plot_rk_density()`. The `n_max` argument adds dashed lines at the centres
of the categories:

```{r density, eval = has_ggplot2}
plot_rk_density(y, tk_max = 5, n_max = 9)
```

```{r density-rk, eval = has_ggplot2}
plot_rk_density(y, what = "rk",
                peaks = c("1_1"))
```

## 3. Classification: `classify_rk()`

`classify_rk()` assigns each ratio to a bin, using all the categories from
`1_n_max` to `n_max_1`. Ratios more extreme than that become `NA`. The
default is `n_max = 5` (categories `1_5` ... `5_1`). In this vignette we
analyse the categories from `1_9` to `9_1`, so we set `n_max = 9`:

```{r classify}
y$bins <- classify_rk(y$rk, n_max = 9)
table(y$bins, useNA = "ifany")
```

To work only on some categories, possibly not contiguous, pass `peaks`.
Ratios outside them become `NA`:

```{r classify-peaks}
table(classify_rk(y$rk, peaks = c("1_2", "1_1", "2_1")), useNA = "ifany")
```

The bins do not all have the same width: `off` bins are wider than `on`
bins, and categories become narrower as `n` grows. Raw counts therefore
cannot be compared across bins directly, which is why the counts are
normalized (step 5).

## 4. Counts per group: `count_rk()`

`count_rk()` counts the bins within each group. Here the counts are pooled
over all the recordings of each individual (`by = ind_id`). In the wide
format (the default) there is one row per group and one column per bin.
`keep_cols` carries along columns that are constant within the group, such
as the sex of the individual.

```{r count}
b <- count_rk(y, by = c(ind_id), bin_col = bins, keep_cols = sex)
b[, 1:9]
```

`format = "long"` gives one row per group x bin instead:

```{r count-long}
b_long <- count_rk(y, by = c(ind_id), bin_col = bins,
                   keep_cols = sex, format = "long")
head(b_long)
```

## 5. Null model and normalization

### The null distribution

Even a random sequence of intervals produces ratios in every bin, with
proportions that depend on the bin widths and on the distribution of the
intervals. `compute_null_distributions()` estimates this baseline, following
Jadoul et al. (2025):

1. fits a distribution to the observed `tk` (`"uniform"`, `"exponential"`,
   `"halfnormal"` or `"lognormal"`);
2. simulates pairs of independent intervals from it;
3. computes and classifies their `rk`;
4. returns the proportion of simulated pairs in each bin.

With `type_col` a separate null model is fitted for each group (here, each
sex). `plot = TRUE` compares the simulated and observed `tk` and shows the
simulated `rk`. The null model must cover the same categories as the
classification, so `n_max = 9` is passed here too. `n_sim = 1e6` (the
default) simulated pairs give stable proportions even for the narrowest
bins.

```{r null, fig.height = 6}
norm_df <- compute_null_distributions(
  y, tk_col = tk, type_col = sex, distribution = "lognormal",
  n_max = 9, n_sim = 1e6, seed = 1, plot = TRUE
)
head(norm_df)
attr(norm_df, "params")
```

### Comparing the null distributions

The choice of the null distribution matters: each one implies a different
baseline for the bins. Below, the four available null models are fitted on
the intervals of both sexes together (no `type_col`). For each one, the
left panel compares the simulated `tk` with the observed `tk` (dashed red
line), and the right panel shows the resulting simulated `rk`.

```{r null-all, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 3.5, results = "hide"}
dists <- c("uniform", "exponential", "halfnormal", "lognormal")
null_all <- lapply(stats::setNames(dists, dists), function(d) {
  compute_null_distributions(y, tk_col = tk, distribution = d,
                             n_max = 9, n_sim = 1e6, seed = 1, plot = TRUE)
})
```

The estimated parameters of each model:

```{r null-all-params}
do.call(rbind, lapply(dists, function(d) {
  cbind(distribution = d, attr(null_all[[d]], "params"))
}))
```

Expected proportion of each bin under the four models (one column per
model):

```{r null-all-table}
null_tab <- data.frame(bin = null_all[[1]]$bin,
                       sapply(null_all, `[[`, "normalization_constant"))
null_tab[-1] <- round(null_tab[-1], 4)
null_tab
```

```{r null-all-plot, fig.height = 4.5}
cols <- c("grey40", "darkorange", "steelblue", "firebrick")
graphics::matplot(as.matrix(null_tab[dists]), type = "o", pch = 16, lty = 1,
                  col = cols, xaxt = "n", xlab = "", ylab = "expected proportion",
                  main = "Bin proportions under each null model")
graphics::axis(1, at = seq_len(nrow(null_tab)), labels = null_tab$bin,
               las = 2, cex.axis = 0.7)
graphics::legend("topright", legend = dists, col = cols, lty = 1, pch = 16,
                 bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
```

```{r null-all-info, include = FALSE}
p11 <- unlist(null_tab[null_tab$bin == "1_1_on", dists])
```

The models mostly disagree around the centre: the expected proportion of
`1_1_on`, for instance, ranges from `r round(min(p11), 3)`
(`r names(which.min(p11))`) to `r round(max(p11), 3)`
(`r names(which.max(p11))`). Since the observed counts are divided by these
proportions, the choice of the null model directly affects the evidence for
the `1_1` category. Choose the model whose simulated `tk` best matches the
observed `tk` in the panels above: here the lognormal one, used in the rest
of this vignette.

### Normalizing the counts

`normalize_rk_counts()` divides each count by the null proportion of its
bin, matching the constants to the rows by `type_col`. The result says how
many times more (or less) often a bin occurs than expected by chance.

```{r normalize}
b_norm <- normalize_rk_counts(b, norm_df, type_col = sex)
b_norm[c("ind_id", "sex", "1_1_on", "1_1_on_norm",
         "1_1_off", "1_1_off_norm")]
```

A simpler alternative, which needs no null model, divides by the width of
each bin in rk units (`method = "width"`), giving a density-like count:

```{r normalize-width}
b_width <- normalize_rk_counts(b, method = "width")
round(unlist(b_width[1, c("1_1_on_norm", "1_1_off_norm")]), 1)
```

The long format is supported too, with `format = "long"` and `bin_col`:

```{r normalize-long}
head(normalize_rk_counts(b_long, norm_df, type_col = sex,
                         format = "long", bin_col = bins))
```

## 6. Testing the categories: `test_peaks()`

For each category, `test_peaks()` runs a paired Wilcoxon test of the
normalized `on` count against the normalized `off` count, across the rows
of `counts` (here, the individuals).

A single null simulation contains Monte Carlo noise, so the test is repeated
over many independent null models generated by `simulate_null_runs()`. The
summary reports how many of the runs give a significant result. A category
can be considered robust when it is significant in (nearly) all runs. Here
we use 20 runs to keep the build time short; in a real analysis use at
least the default (`runs = 100`).

All the categories from `1_9` to `9_1` are tested (`n_max = 9`, the same
used in `classify_rk()`). Males and females are analysed together: without
`type_col`, a single null model is fitted on all the intervals and each
category is tested once, on all the individuals.

```{r runs-all}
norm_runs_all <- simulate_null_runs(y, tk_col = tk,
                                    distribution = "lognormal", n_max = 9,
                                    n_sim = 1e6, runs = 20, seed = 1,
                                    verbose = FALSE)
res_all <- test_peaks(b, norm_runs_all, verbose = FALSE)
res_all$summary
```

```{r test-info, include = FALSE}
robust <- res_all$summary[!is.na(res_all$summary$prop) & res_all$summary$prop >= 0.95, ]
robust_txt <- if (nrow(robust) == 0) {
  "no category is significant in at least 95% of the runs"
} else {
  paste0("the categories significant in at least 95% of the runs are ",
         paste0(robust$test, " (", robust$sig, "/", robust$n_run, ")",
                collapse = "; "))
}
```

`sig` is the number of runs with `p < alpha` (0.05 by default), and
`perc` / `prop` express it as a percentage / proportion of the valid runs
(`n_run`). In this example `r robust_txt`. A category significant in only
a fraction of the runs is not a robust result, because it depends on the
particular null simulation.

`$p_values` contains the p-value of every run x category:

```{r test-p}
head(res_all$p_values)
```

Use `alternative = "less"` (on < off) or `"two.sided"` to test other
hypotheses. With `type_col = sex` (in both `simulate_null_runs()` and
`test_peaks()`) a null model is fitted and the tests are run separately for
each sex; `by` splits the tests by other columns as well.

## 7. Locating the peaks: `find_rk_peaks()`

`find_rk_peaks()` estimates the density of `rk` once and returns, for each
category, the position of the density maximum within the category's range.
It is useful to check whether the observed peaks fall close to the integer
ratios:

```{r peaks}
pk <- find_rk_peaks(y$rk, peaks = c("1_1"))
pk
```

```{r peaks-info, include = FALSE}
# a maximum within 1% of the range width from an edge is not a local peak
tol <- 0.01 * (pk$range_max - pk$range_min)
at_edge <- pk$peak_x - pk$range_min < tol | pk$range_max - pk$peak_x < tol
inner_txt <- if (any(!at_edge)) {
  paste0("Here ", paste0(pk$peak[!at_edge], " (", round(pk$peak_x[!at_edge], 3), ")",
                         collapse = ", "),
         " has a real peak inside its range")
} else {
  "Here no category has a peak inside its range"
}
edge_txt <- if (any(at_edge)) {
  paste0(", while for ", paste(pk$peak[at_edge], collapse = ", "),
         " the maximum lies at the edge")
} else ""
```

Look at `peak_x` together with `range_min` / `range_max`. When the maximum
lies at the edge of the range, the density keeps rising or falling across
the whole category. There is then no local peak inside it: the reported
value only marks the side the density is coming from. Only a `peak_x` well
inside the range indicates a real mode close to the category.
`r inner_txt``r edge_txt`.

## 8. Three consecutive intervals: `plot_rk_ternary()`

`rk` looks at two intervals at a time. `plot_rk_ternary()` looks at three
consecutive intervals `(tk1, tk2, tk3)` and places each triplet in a ternary
diagram according to the relative duration of the three. Isochronous
triplets fall in the centre. This plot requires the **ggtern** package.

```{r ternary, eval = has_ggtern, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
plot_rk_ternary(y, tk_col = tk, by = c(file_id, ind_id),
                order_col = onset, tk_max = 5)
```

## Practical notes

- **Simultaneous onsets.** Two events with the same onset give `tk = 0`,
  hence `rk = 0` or `rk = 1`, which fall outside every category (`NA` in
  `classify_rk()`). `compute_null_distributions()` ignores intervals
  `<= 0` when fitting the null model.
- **Negative intervals.** If you supply your own `tk`, `calculate_rk()`
  warns about negative values and does not compute the ratios involving
  them.
- **Choosing `n_max`.** Use the same `n_max` in `classify_rk()` and in the
  null model. Bins beyond the `n_max` of the null model have no
  normalization constant, and `test_peaks()` reports the categories it
  could not test.
- **Few data per group.** `compute_null_distributions()` warns when a
  `type_col` group has fewer than 10 intervals, since its null model is
  then poorly estimated.

## Reference

Jadoul, Y., Tufarelli, T., Coissac, C., Gamba, M., & Ravignani, A. (2025).
Hidden assumptions of integer ratio analyses in bioacoustics and music.
*Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences*, 1553(1), 363-378.
